title: Consistent Hashing: Complete Architecture
description: Design a consistent hashing ring with virtual nodes to minimize key remapping when servers join or leave.

data.text: Design a partitioning scheme for a distributed cache that must keep keys mapped to servers when the fleet changes. With naive modulo hashing (`hash(key) % N`), adding or removing a server remaps nearly every key and causes a massive cache miss storm. The scheme must spread keys evenly across heterogeneous servers, minimize remapping on membership changes, and support replication.

terms.definition: A circular space of size 2^m. Keys and servers are both hashed onto this ring, and a key is mapped to the next server encountered moving clockwise.
Each physical server is represented by multiple points on the ring, so a server with more capacity gets more points and the key distribution becomes far more uniform.
When a server joins, only the keys from its predecessor on the ring move to it. When it leaves, only its keys move to its successor. Most keys stay put.
Alternative non-ring hashing schemes. Rendezvous is easy to compute and has good distribution; Jump Hash is minimal-memory but only supports nodes in a fixed sequence.
A server that receives disproportionately many keys due to poor hash distribution or an unlucky ring layout.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Key Placement: for any key, deterministically find the responsible server(s)
Dynamic Membership: support adding and removing servers with minimal key rebalancing
Replication: write to the primary and the next N-1 distinct servers on the ring
Weighting: assign more virtual nodes to larger instances so capacity is respected
Lookup API: given a key, return the ordered list of replica servers in under a microsecond

data.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items: Even Distribution: standard deviation under 2% of the mean across all servers
Minimal Disruption: add one server -> move only ~1/N of keys, not ~all
Low Lookup Cost: ring lookup in O(log V) with binary search over V virtual nodes
Stateless Clients: clients can compute the target server themselves without a central router
Avoid Hotspots: resist adversarial keys and natural clustering

data.text: Both keys and server endpoints are hashed onto a ring of integers modulo 2^32 or 2^64. Walking clockwise from the key's hash position hits the first server hash — that server owns the key.

data.text: Without virtual nodes, a small number of server positions on the ring leaves large gaps and causes skew. With virtual nodes, each physical server gets many random points, and a larger server gets proportionally more to match its capacity.

faqs.question: How many virtual nodes should each server have?
faqs.answer: 100-200 virtual nodes is typical for caches and object stores. More virtual nodes give better uniformity but increase the size of the ring (more points to search) and memory. For large fleets, 64 is sometimes enough; for small fleets, 256 improves evenness.

faqs.question: What hash function should be used?
faqs.answer: Use a non-cryptographic, fast hash like MurmurHash3 or xxHash. MD5 and SHA are too slow for per-request routing. The goal is good avalanche distribution, not cryptographic strength.

faqs.question: How do clients learn about ring changes?
faqs.answer: Options: push updates from a control plane (zookeeper/etcd) to all clients, or have clients discover membership via a service registry and rebuild their local ring periodically. For stateless clients that compute the target themselves, pushing a compact ring snapshot is cheap (each vnode is a pair of 8-byte hash and server id).

faqs.question: What about hotspots caused by a specific key?
faqs.answer: Consistent hashing avoids hotspotting from membership changes, but it cannot stop an adversarial client from hammering one key. Combine with key salting (append a random suffix) only if replicas are read in parallel, or use a per-key rate limit / hot-key caching. Never rely on consistent hashing alone to fix hot keys.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Consistent hashing limits remapping to the arc when servers change, unlike modulo hashing
Virtual nodes smooth the distribution and allow weighting by server capacity
Replication is a natural extension: walk clockwise to the next N distinct physical nodes
Clients can route without a proxy by holding a local copy of the ring
Even distribution requires both a good hash function and enough virtual nodes
data.takeaway: Consistent hashing turns a brittle modulo partition into a stable ring where most keys stay put on membership changes, with virtual nodes making it uniform enough for production.
